title: Google DeepMind Gives AI-Designed Proteins a Watermark
key_facts: Google DeepMind's SynthID Bio is a method that sneaks a subtle signal (a watermark) into AI-designed proteins during the design process; it is adapted from SynthID-Text (2024) and could be built into protein-design systems such as AlphaFold and RFdiffusion.

Two problems it targets: biosecurity (an AI-designed sequence far from known ones could slip past DNA-synthesis screening, which compares ordered sequences with a database of controlled sequences) and 'biological AI slop' (AI-generated structures polluting databases scientists rely on).

It nudges design choices such as which amino acid comes next and slightly shifts atom positions; it fine-tunes a small part of AlphaFold3 so proteins generated by the model carry the watermark whoever runs it.

DeepMind generated protein binders aimed at several targets (immune regulation, blood vessel growth, viral proteins); in lab tests the watermarked versions performed as well as unwatermarked ones, which the team calls the first watermarked and biologically functional protein binders.
Limits: the watermark can be scrubbed if a marked protein is run through another design tool to produce a similar new sequence, and SynthID Bio cannot currently identify who created a protein.

Outside views: Oliver Crook (University of Oxford) told Science that for researchers on non-sensitive questions the marking could be 'added complexity'; James Diggans (Twist Bioscience, not involved but gave early feedback) said DNA synthesis companies have an important role; a survey of 130 stakeholders reached no consensus on who should get the decoder key.

DeepMind is releasing its SynthID Bio code and experimental data to researchers, and with Arc Institute and Stanford University has watermarked the genomes of AI-designed bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) without disabling them, in early tests.
quote_evidence: To prevent this, AI-designed proteins could soon carry a watermark.
But there’s a catch: The watermark can be scrubbed.
Also, SynthID Bio can’t currently be used to identify the creator of a protein, limiting its ability to trace illicit use or to mark intellectual property.
why_it_matters_hint: A watermark could help DNA-synthesis screeners and database keepers tell AI-designed proteins from natural ones, but it can be scrubbed, cannot name the creator and has no agreed key holder.
event_date: DeepMind announced SynthID Bio on 30 Sep 2026 (DeepMind's own post, dated 30 Sep 2026); the article is dated 5 Oct 2026.
